title: How Government Shutdowns Work
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain how US federal government shutdowns work. They cover the constitutional power of the purse and Article One, the Anti-Deficiency Act of 1884, the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act under Nixon in 1974, the annual appropriations process (budget request, concurrent resolution, twelve appropriations subcommittee bills, omnibus packages, October 1 fiscal year deadline), continuing resolutions and policy riders, funding gaps, Attorney General Benjamin Civiletti's 1981 opinion that made shutdowns real, the 1995-96 Clinton-Gingrich shutdowns, the 2013 Ted Cruz-led shutdown over the Affordable Care Act, and the 2018-2019 Trump border wall shutdown lasting 35 days. They discuss furloughs, unpaid and lost back pay, essential workers such as the Coast Guard and TSA, and effects on national parks, food inspections, and travelers. Closing listener mail corrects a slip about the Swedish prime minister and a math question about nine thousand seconds.
topics: Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act

segments.title: Tour dates and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts promote upcoming live shows in Orlando, New Orleans, Chicago and Austin, then banter about caffeine and the episode's timing before introducing the topic of government shutdowns.

segments.title: What a shutdown is and the power of the purse
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck define a federal government shutdown as agencies losing funding and so being unable to pay workers. They cite Article One, Section Nine of the Constitution giving Congress control of spending, and the presidents' workaround of contracting first and asking Congress to pay later.

segments.title: Anti-Deficiency Act and Nixon's budget reform
segments.summary: The 1884 Anti-Deficiency Act closed the loophole by barring spending that Congress had not appropriated. The 1974 Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act then set up the budgeting process used today.
topics: Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act

segments.title: Annual appropriations process
segments.summary: The president's budget request is due in early February, though it is not binding. Congress passes a concurrent budget resolution by mid-April, the Appropriations Committees divide spending into twelve bills, subcommittees negotiate, and the bills may be combined into an omnibus package. The deadline is October 1, and Congress has met it only four times since 1977.

segments.title: Continuing resolutions
segments.summary: When appropriations bills are not passed by October 1, Congress often passes a continuing resolution that keeps spending at the prior year's levels. Policy riders can be attached. Since 1977 there have been 186 continuing resolutions, 117 of them since 1990.

segments.title: Show tangent on the TV series Veep
segments.summary: Hosts briefly praise the show Veep for depicting Washington dealmaking and mention a personal anecdote about actress Julia Louis-Dreyfus.

segments.title: Funding gaps and the 1981 Civiletti opinion
segments.summary: Most funding gaps are short, often over a weekend. Medicaid funding for abortion was a 1977 and 1978 sticking point. Attorney General Benjamin Civiletti said under the Anti-Deficiency Act agencies could not keep operating during a shutdown, which made shutdowns real and less frequent.

segments.title: Major shutdowns: 1995-96, 2013, and 2018-19
segments.summary: The 1995-96 shutdowns between Clinton and Gingrich over the Contract with America lasted 26 days combined, with Republicans blamed. The 2013 shutdown lasted 16 days, led by Ted Cruz over the Affordable Care Act. The 2018-19 partial shutdown over Trump's border wall funding lasted 35 days, the longest on record, and ended with the public blaming the president.

segments.title: Economic and personal costs, furloughs and back pay
segments.summary: Shutdowns cost the economy money and federal workers lose pay that is often never recovered. In the 2018-19 shutdown about 800,000 workers were affected, and some essential workers such as TSA and Coast Guard staff worked unpaid. Congress members keep pay. Effects spread to national parks, food inspections, and travelers.

segments.title: How shutdowns differ by agency and wider impact
segments.summary: Each shutdown differs because some appropriations bills may already be passed. Agencies submit contingency plans to OMB. The longer a shutdown lasts, the more programs like SNAP, WIC-type breakfast programs and passport processing are affected. Food inspections slow, and Joshua Tree National Park suffered damage during the most recent shutdown.

segments.title: Listener mail corrections
segments.summary: Listeners correct a mistake about which Swedish prime minister Donald Trump called regarding the arrest of A$AP Rocky, and ask where a figure of nine thousand seconds converting to 104 days came from.
